faq.title: What is a 2-Layer Transistor Pixel CMOS sensor?
faq.description: In conventional CMOS image sensors, the light-capturing photodiode and its accompanying pixel transistors (reset transistor, transfer gate, amplifier) reside side-by-side on the exact same silicon layer, forcing them to compete for surface area. Sony's 2-Layer Transistor Pixel technology (commercialized as 'Exmor T') separates the photodiodes onto an upper silicon substrate and moves the pixel transistors to a separate lower substrate, connecting them via 3D Cu-Cu (copper-to-copper) micro-bonding.

faq.title: How does separating photodiodes and transistors double dynamic range?
faq.description: By moving transistors to a lower substrate, the photodiode can occupy almost 100% of the upper surface area, doubling its physical volume. This approximately doubles the Full-Well Capacity (FWC)—the maximum number of photo-electrons a pixel can hold before clipping. At the same time, the amplifier transistors on the lower substrate can be made significantly larger, slashing electrical read noise by 50% in dark shadow areas.

faq.title: What smartphones currently use 2-Layer Transistor Pixel sensors?
faq.description: Sony debuted the technology in the Xperia 1 V/VI (Exmor T for mobile). It is now being widely adopted across modern flagship camera sensors from Sony (LYTIA LYT-800, LYT-900 series) and competing solutions from Samsung ISOCELL and OmniVision.

html:
Modern smartphone photography has spent a decade engaged in a relentless battle against the laws of optical physics. In a professional full-frame mirrorless camera, a physical sensor measuring 36mm x 24mm gathers vast quantities of photons through wide glass lenses. In an ultra-slim smartphone measuring 8 millimeters thick, physical camera sensor real estate is constrained to tiny fractions of an inch (typically 1/1.3" to 1/1.5").

To overcome microscopic physical sizes, smartphone manufacturers historically pushed megapixel counts higher (48MP, 108MP, 200MP) while relying on complex computational HDR burst stacking to combat sensor noise. However, pixel dimensions shrunk to sub-micron scales (0.6 to 0.8 micrometers), creating severe physical limitations in Full-Well Capacity and Amplifier Read Noise. In response, Sony Semiconductor Solutions introduced the most significant architectural breakthrough in solid-state imaging in 15 years: The 2-Layer Transistor Pixel Stacked CMOS Sensor (commercialized as Exmor T and modern LYTIA sensors). In this technical deep dive, we dissect the semiconductor physics, copper-to-copper 3D hybrid bonding, and dynamic range equations of next-gen mobile image sensors.

The Planar Bottleneck of Conventional Back-Illuminated (BSI) CMOS

To appreciate Sony's architectural innovation, one must inspect the internal anatomy of a conventional Back-Illuminated (BSI) CMOS Image Sensor:

The Four-Transistor (4T) Pixel Architecture:

In standard CMOS sensors, each individual pixel does not merely contain a light-sensitive photodiode; it requires an active electrical circuit to read the captured electrons. In the industry-standard 4T pixel design, each pixel contains:

  1. The Photodiode (PD): Converts incoming photons into electrical electrons via the photoelectric effect.
  2. The Transfer Gate (TG): Moves accumulated electrons from the photodiode to the Floating Diffusion (FD) node.
  3. The Reset Transistor (RST): Clears the floating diffusion node to reference voltage between exposures.
  4. The Amplifying Source Follower (AMP / SF): A field-effect transistor that converts the tiny electron charge into a readable analog voltage signal.
  5. The Row Select Transistor (SEL): Connects the pixel output to the vertical readout column.

The Real Estate Conflict:

In all conventional BSI sensors, the photodiode and these four pixel transistors are manufactured side-by-side on the exact same horizontal silicon substrate plane! As smartphone pixels shrunk to 0.8um and 1.0um, the photodiode and the transistors engaged in a destructive physical compromise:

  • If engineers expand the photodiode area to capture more light, the amplifier transistor must shrink. A smaller amplifier transistor introduces severe RTS (Random Telegraph Signal) Noise and flicker noise, creating ugly color speckles in dark shadow areas.
  • If engineers enlarge the amplifier transistor to suppress noise, the photodiode's physical volume shrinks. A tiny photodiode can only store a tiny number of electrons before overflowing (clipping highlights), destroying the sensor's optical dynamic range!

For more technical details on how sensor optics interact with lens zoom, check out our guide on periscope optical zoom vs in-sensor crop in smartphone cameras.

The Architectural Breakthrough: 2-Layer Transistor Pixel Technology

Sony's 2-Layer Transistor Pixel architecture completely resolves this physical compromise by turning a planar two-dimensional chip into a Three-Dimensional Stacked Semiconductor Sandwich.

Separating Photodiodes and Transistors via 3D Cu-Cu Hybrid Bonding:

Instead of cramming the photodiode and its readout transistors side-by-side, Sony manufactures them on two completely separate silicon wafer layers:

  1. The Upper Silicon Layer (100% Photodiodes): Dedicated almost exclusively to light absorption. Photodiodes expand to occupy virtually the entire surface area of the pixel, unobstructed by transistors or metal wiring. Furthermore, the physical depth of the silicon photodiode can be extended deeper into the wafer, dramatically increasing absorption of longer red and near-infrared wavelengths.
  2. The Lower Silicon Layer (Pixel Transistors): Houses the reset transistors, transfer gates, and amplifying source followers. Because this layer is freed from light-gathering duties, the amplifier transistors can be expanded by over 200% to 300% in physical size!
  3. The Base Logic Layer: Beneath the transistor layer sits a third silicon layer hosting high-speed Analog-to-Digital Converters (ADCs), digital signal processors (DSP), and mobile MIPI interfaces.

The upper photodiode layer and the lower transistor layer are bonded together at atomic scales using Cu-Cu (Copper-to-Copper) Direct Hybrid Bonding. Microscopic copper pads with sub-micron pitches bond together under heat and pressure, establishing high-bandwidth, ultra-low-resistance electrical vias between each photodiode and its respective amplifier.

The Physics of Dynamic Range: Full-Well Capacity (FWC) and SNR

The quantitative photographic impact of 2-Layer Transistor Pixel architecture is profound. Sensor dynamic range is defined as the ratio between the maximum saturation signal and the minimum noise floor:

\[ ext{Dynamic Range (dB)} = 20 \log_{10} \left( rac{ ext{Full-Well Capacity (electrons)}}{ ext{Total Read Noise Floor (electrons)}} ight)\]

Doubling the Full-Well Capacity (FWC):

Full-Well Capacity (FWC) represents the maximum number of photo-electrons a single pixel's photodiode can accumulate before saturation (where highlight details burn out to pure white). By dedicating the entire upper substrate layer to the photodiode, Sony approximately doubles the Full-Well Capacity per unit area! A 1.12-micrometer 2-layer pixel can hold as many electrons as a conventional 1.6-micrometer pixel, preserving nuanced cloud textures, neon sign colors, and bright sunsets without digital clipping.

Halving the Read Noise Floor:

Concurrently, because the amplifying source follower transistor on the lower layer is significantly larger, thermal flicker noise and channel resistance fluctuations plummet. The sensor's read noise drops by approximately 50%. Doubling the numerator (FWC) while halving the denominator (read noise) yields an astronomical 2 to 3-stop expansion in pure linear optical dynamic range! A 1/1.4" mobile sensor built with 2-layer technology delivers low-light signal-to-noise ratios (SNR) that rival conventional 1-inch smartphone camera sensors.

Dual Conversion Gain (DCG) Switching Physics

In addition to 2-layer stacking, modern sensors like the Sony LYT-800/900 series incorporate Dual Conversion Gain (DCG) inside the transistor layer:

  • High Conversion Gain (HCG): In low-light environments, the pixel switches to a microscopic floating diffusion capacitance. A tiny electrical charge generates a massive voltage swing, elevating the signal far above thermal circuit noise, producing clean, noiseless shadow detail.
  • Low Conversion Gain (LCG): In bright direct sunlight, the pixel switches to a large floating diffusion capacitance, allowing the pixel to absorb thousands of additional electrons without saturating highlights.

Comparison: Mobile CMOS Sensor Architectural Generations

Review the evolution of mobile image sensor semiconductor physics:

Parameter Front-Illuminated (FSI) Back-Illuminated (BSI) 2-Layer Transistor (Exmor T)
Pixel Layout Metal wiring above silicon Planar Photodiode + Transistor 3D Stacked: Separate Substrates
Photodiode Surface Ratio ~30% - 40% ~50% - 60% ~90% - 95% (Near Total)
Full-Well Capacity (FWC) Low (Easily clips) Standard Baseline 2x Higher per unit area
Amplifier Noise Floor High Noise Moderate (Constrained gates) Ultra-Low (Enlarged gates)
Dynamic Range 60 - 65 dB 70 - 75 dB 82 - 86+ dB (Single Exposure)

Conclusion: The Future of Mobile Optical Fidelity

Sony's 2-Layer Transistor Pixel architecture represents a historic triumph of semiconductor manufacturing over physical dimensional constraints. By moving from planar compromise to 3D vertical stacking, modern smartphone cameras capture clean, natural, and filmic high-dynamic-range imagery straight from raw silicon—drastically reducing the need for aggressive, artificial computational post-processing and elevating mobile photography into a true professional medium.

Deep Trench Isolation (DTI) and Optical Cross-Talk Physics

As smartphone camera pixel pitches shrunk to 1.0 micrometer and below, a severe optical defect threatened image clarity: Optical and Electrical Cross-Talk. When light strikes a photodiode at an angle (especially near the edges of a camera lens), photons can bleed sideways into adjacent pixel diodes. Red photons leak into green pixels, resulting in color contamination, muddy skin tones, and smeared details.

To eliminate cross-talk in modern 2-Layer Transistor sensors, semiconductor foundries utilize Full Deep Trench Isolation (FDTI). Engineers etch microscopic physical vertical trenches completely through the silicon between adjacent pixels, filling the trenches with high-reflectivity dielectric materials (like silicon dioxide). These trenches act as microscopic optical mirrors: photons that attempt to bleed into neighboring pixels are reflected back into their own photodiode. FDTI boosts color separation by 40% and preserves razor-sharp optical contrast across every pixel on the sensor.

Conversion Gain Switching and Automotive High-Dynamic-Range Sensors

The architectural benefits of 2-layer stacked CMOS technology are now revolutionizing automotive safety and autonomous driving vision. In advanced driver-assistance systems (ADAS), cameras must instantly see both the blinding glare of oncoming high-beam LED headlights and pedestrians walking in pitch-black shadow zones simultaneously.

Stacked CMOS sensors achieve over 120 to 140 dB of single-exposure dynamic range by reading the high-conversion gain and low-conversion gain capacitor registers concurrently. By fusing these two signals inside the on-chip base logic layer in real time, the sensor delivers motion-artifact-free video that completely eliminates the ghosting and motion blur caused by traditional multi-frame exposure bracketing!

Quantum Efficiency (QE) Optimization Across Spectral Bands

In addition to noise reduction, 2-layer transistor sensors significantly improve Quantum Efficiency (QE)—the percentage of photons striking the sensor that successfully generate measurable electrons. Conventional mobile sensors typically achieve 60% to 70% QE in green light, but drop to under 40% in deep red and near-infrared (NIR) wavelengths.

By deepening the silicon photodiode volume on the isolated upper wafer layer, photons have a longer physical absorption path length before escaping. Quantum efficiency across red and near-infrared bands surges to over 85%. This provides night photography with richer color saturation, sharper star fields in mobile astrophotography, and dramatically clearer autofocus tracking in moonlit environments.
